evidence.title: Buzz 1.0.6 human input and ownership inspection

evidence.title: Buzz 1.0.6 supplied delegation instructions and tools

criteria.result: Buzz 1.0.6 has macOS, Windows and Linux desktop builds and a bundled CLI. The companion iPhone and Android apps can reach the same agents; production browser and editor-extension clients are absent from the scoped app distribution.

Buzz 1.0.6 integrates Claude Code, Codex, Goose and opt-in Pi locally, plus shared Mesh inference and Builderlab hosted agents. The 0.X Cursor, Grok Build and OpenCode presets are not in this release.

Local Claude and Codex use provider sign-in/subscriptions; Goose and Pi accept provider credentials. Builderlab adds prepaid hosted inference and compute, with separate account and US eligibility restrictions.

Install Buzz, choose or migrate a key identity, join/create a community, configure a harness and send a mention or Solo prompt. Local folders need no remote Git account; managed communities and remote agents use Builderlab.

Buzz 1.0.6 bundles relay CLI operations and exposes agent tools through its local bridge. Relay REST/WebSocket interfaces, preview plugin APIs and hosted integrations have different authentication and stability boundaries.
Trusted plugins add pages, tools, agent types and execution providers. MCP connections and instructions may come from the selected harness; hosted service connections belong to Builderlab.

Buzz 1.0.6 desktop is Tauri 2 with React web UI. The companion mobile source remains Flutter with native platform integrations in block/buzz. A web-rendered UI does not establish a production browser client.

Buzz 1.0 intake is conversational. The bundled CLI also creates native relay issues with stable signed IDs; the app browses repository/external issues but does not restore the removed issue editor or synchronize an external tracker.

A conversation Canvas can hold a durable brief and links, editable by people or agents. It is a general shared document, with no separate acceptance-criteria object or implementation-linked task-plan lifecycle.

Buzz 1.0.6 has conversations, agent teams and flat CLI relay issues. It supplies no native epic/dependency graph or task-to-epic lifecycle; channel and team grouping do not establish those operations.

Buzz supplies agent/team/workspace instructions, shared Canvas context and community-scoped agent memory. The pinned release supports memory tools and versioned writes; it does not establish the Memory tab described on the live support page.

Agents can search accessible conversations, browse repository content and use their harness’s file tools. Buzz 1.0.6 does not supply a semantic repository index or an architecture/specification conflict gate.

Native issues remain available through the CLI bundled in v1.0.6, with creation, labels, assignment, filtering and durable status. The desktop app no longer has the Todos/0.X issue editor or an epic backlog UI.

People and agents can use the same bundled CLI to create, read, assign and change native relay issue records. The 1.0 UI can browse/share repository issues, but has no native task-board editing or dependency operations.
Canvas and notes can retain requirements and links across conversations, but Buzz 1.0.6 has no maintained product-spec object with approval, implementation coverage or drift/review enforcement.

Separate local/hosted agents can work concurrently. In v1.0.6 each local agent has a serial mention lane plus up to eight Attention Interest lanes; this replaces the old 0.X configurable ACP-pool description.

Mentions/DMs route agent work; a bounded local runner orders it and prevents duplicate same-device custody. CLI issue self-assignment is separate from conversation dispatch and does not impose a distributed work lock.

Buzz supplies delegation/callback instructions and messaging tools for agents to assign work in shared channels and return results. Agent creation requires owner review, and the UI does not turn exchanges into a parent/child task tree.

Relay workflows handle cron/message/reaction/diff/webhook automation. Local agents also own Attention Interests with event, timer and plugin-source watches; local work stops with the app, while relay/hosted execution has a separate lifetime.

Desktop offers stop, follow-ups, interrupted-turn resume, Attention pause and visible errors. Ordinary coding turns bypass interactive command approval; owner-reviewed drafts and experimental protection are separate decision paths.
Agents, conversations, Activity, Usage and workflow run views expose agent work, but v1.0.6 has no epic fleet board or task dependency/parent-child model. No multi-epic usability fixture was run.

A direct prompt starts work without a mandatory workflow. Per-agent harness/model/instructions, channel templates and owner-reviewed natural-language configuration are available; there is no growing-epic lifecycle or orchestration tree.

Local agents need Buzz running on their host. Builderlab hosted agents use paid remote workstations and can respond while the desktop is off; relay self-hosting and custom execution adapters are separate BYO operations.

Local agents run with app-user OS authority, with project folders and optional Git worktrees/branches for file separation. Remote execution providers and Builderlab workstation sharing are separate boundaries; hosted VM/container internals are not public.

Buzz retains conversation/session identity and interrupted-turn receipts, rather than the 0.X nonpersistent ACP pool. Closing the app still ends local execution; supported turns can resume, while missing remote targets require a deliberate new session.

Buzz installs/configures supported harnesses and can reuse hosted workstations or plugin-supplied remote targets. It does not supply a general local dependency/cache/port manager for parallel projects.

The 1.0.6 runner bounds queue length, admission rate and requested turn deadlines; runtime errors and failed watches have explicit handling. Local token/spend budgets remain provider-owned; hosted services can stop or throttle at an insufficient prepaid balance.

Activity, transcripts, workflow run traces and optional Usage expose work/errors and local session statistics. These do not supply native issue/epic delivery statistics or measured catalog performance claims.

Opt-in Usage shows local session/descendant tokens and estimated API-list costs, with known gaps and thread drill-down. Builderlab separately bills pooled compute/inference/data; local estimates are not a task-level invoice.

The local runner bounds mention/Attention work and coordinates same-device custody; Builderlab sizes remote computers separately. No host-resource scheduler or deduplicated verification service is supplied by the inspected app.

Buzz has shared attributed conversations, presence, membership and read/write roles. Local coding-agent invocation remains owner/verified-sibling controlled, so shared chat is not proof that two people can steer the same coding process.

Community/channel membership and named roles control shared access; Builderlab workspace admin controls hosted resources and funds. Enterprise advertises SSO, distinct from local key custody and self-host relay operator roles.

Ordinary local Claude/Codex turns use broad host access and bypass interactive approvals. Owner-reviewed plugin/agent drafts and experimental protection providers are distinct from the unimplemented relay workflow approval gate and disabled external-app consent feature.

Signed relay messages, edits, membership and workflow records preserve attributed activity subject to operator retention. Native issue/agent decisions and GitHub reviews are separate objects; no immutable cross-product decision ledger is asserted.

Buzz 1.0.6 has local change cards and a GitHub side panel with diffs, checks, reviews and next merge actions. This is an individual change/PR workflow, without a native task-review queue or measured reviewer-usability study.

Sharing a conversation exposes its retained history/Canvas, and using the same agent preserves community memory. It does not transfer ownership, local credentials or live runtime authority to a second person; exporting an agent creates a separate identity without memory/history.

Buzz retains conversation attachments/Canvas and exposes local per-turn change cards, diff cards, hosted apps and GitHub review panels. It does not supply a unified cross-task artifact gallery or guaranteed exact-revision evidence for every output.

Buzz’s shipped prompt asks agents to verify work, while GitHub panels expose repository checks/reviews. These are distinct from product-enforced tests, lint, type or persistent-spec gates on every completed task.

Buzz 1.0.6 offers worktree instructions, local change snapshots, bundled native relay PR commands and a GitHub panel for reviews/checks/merge actions. General Git commits and conflict repair remain harness/user work.

GitHub reviews, merge/enqueue/auto-merge and branch updates use the signed-in account and displayed commit. Builderlab app deployments use separate account tools; neither implies a universal product release/production approval gate.

PRs and hosted apps retain source/deployment references and conversations can hold result evidence. Buzz 1.0.6 has no universal native task-to-build/delivery ledger or rollback model; individual GitHub actions are bound to their displayed head.

Buzz provides individual diff/PR review, change-request actions and GitHub’s merge queue. It does not supply a coordinated high-volume native task-review/release queue with dependency/risk grouping or verification deduplication.

The Buzz 1.0.6 app and separately pinned relay are Apache-2.0 with third-party notices. Open source for those components does not establish the license or deployment parity of all Builderlab-hosted services.

Buzz’s app and independently operated relay remain usable without Builderlab. Hosted communities, remote agents, apps and billing use Builderlab; agent setup exports and privacy portability requests are narrower than a complete hosted-history migration.

Local keys/harness data, relay content and Builderlab-operated services have different handling. Hosted content and provider transmission/retention are documented; local diagnostics controls do not establish a global service telemetry switch.

Community/local software is free, while Builderlab Pay as you go adds a free workspace allowance beside metered data, compute and inference. Enterprise is a custom agreement; the old claim of no paid Buzz offering is superseded.

Hosted compute has explicit unit rates and shared allowances, but the catalog has no measured fixed-workload token/call/runtime trace for one, two or five developers. Scenario totals therefore remain partial rather than invented averages.

Buzz 1.0.6 is the November 20 successor desktop release, with later 1.0.7 previews tracked separately. Public source/support channels and early-stage limits are documented; no GA reliability or universal response-time promise is inferred.

Enterprise SSO/dedicated tenancy/custom SLA is not proof of ISO certification or a SOC 2 report. The checked public pricing, support, privacy materials do not identify a Buzz/Builderlab certificate or audit report with scope and dates.

Buzz offers free open-source local/self-host access and a Pay as you go workspace with no payment method to start. Paid remote compute/inference is separate; a prepaid top-up is neither a paid-only app nor a one-time software licence.

Pay as you go publishes data/compute units, allowances and model pricing by reference; Enterprise is quote-only. Compute infrastructure markup and a universal tax-inclusive scenario bill are not disclosed. Prepaid credits are consumption funding, not a one-time licence.
